pre_match.market_prob_basis: Pre-match market price on Argentina: ~-675 American / ~87% implied (Caesars/FOX Bet, per seed). Corroborated by FanDuel's -650 moneyline (raw 86.7% three-way, vig+draw not stripped) reported by FanDuel Research and FOX Sports. Kept at the seed's 0.871 as the market-implied figure; Opta's supercomputer (a model, not a market) put Argentina at 80.2% — surfaced in the odds layer.

odds.text: Bookmaker market: Argentina ~-675/-650 American on the moneyline, ~87% implied (FOX Bet/Caesars/FanDuel) — kept as market_prob 0.871. As an independent model cross-check, the Opta supercomputer's Monte-Carlo simulation priced the match Argentina 80.2% / Draw 12.9% / Saudi Arabia 6.9% pre-match. Both real systems agreed Argentina was a heavy favourite; the result (Saudi 6.9% per Opta) was one of the most improbable in World Cup history and a near-worst-case Brier outcome for any favourite-backing forecaster.

narrative.storyline: Renard's high line weaponised — Argentina drowned in offsides
narrative.text: Hervé Renard kept Saudi Arabia's back four pushed aggressively high all match, daring Argentina to run in behind. It backfired on Argentina: per Opta, Argentina were flagged offside six times inside the first 32 minutes — more than any team managed in a full match at the entire 2018 World Cup — and seven times before half-time. The trap turned Argentina's pace and through-ball game into a self-defeating weapon and choked the midfield space Messi works in.
narrative.why: The single tactical mechanism that decided the game: it neutralised Argentina's chance-creation edge and chalked off goals, letting a 0.14-xG Saudi side stay level long enough to win.

narrative.storyline: Three Argentina goals chalked off — Lautaro twice, margins of millimetres
narrative.text: Argentina had the ball in the net three more times and saw all three ruled out for offside via semi-automated technology — two of them Lautaro Martínez goals decided by an armpit/shoulder being marginal inches beyond the last defender. Fans and analysts argued at least one (with left-back Yasser Al-Shahrani appearing to play Lautaro on) was harshly called. Had any stood, the upset likely never happens.
narrative.why: The fine-margin turning point: the scoreline that looked like comfortable Argentine control was actually held to 1-0 by millimetric VAR lines, leaving the door open.

narrative.storyline: Renard's halftime masterstroke and Saudi grit after going 1-0 down
narrative.text: Despite an early Messi penalty and relentless first-half pressure, Renard did not retreat — he doubled down on the high press at the break, crushing the space between Saudi lines and refusing to sit deep. Saudi Arabia, who had zero shots in the first half, came out and struck twice in five minutes, riding a wave of belief and physical commitment (they out-fouled Argentina 21 to 7) to hold the line for 37+ minutes after taking the lead.
narrative.why: The human/motivation story behind the comeback: a coach's nerve and a squad's collective resolve converting a hopeless xG profile into a famous win.

narrative.storyline: Messi's last-dance opener and the end of a 36-game unbeaten run
narrative.text: Messi converted a 10th-minute penalty (won via VAR for Saud Abdulhamid's shirt-pull on Paredes) to become the fifth player to score at four different World Cups — a dream start to his final World Cup. By full time it was a nightmare: Argentina's 36-match unbeaten run was over, drawing comparisons to Cameroon shocking Maradona's Argentina in 1990, and casting immediate doubt over the eventual champions' campaign.
narrative.why: The human arc and stakes — the tournament's defining what-the-hell moment for the eventual winners, and the personal weight on Messi's last World Cup.

magic_moment.text: Al-Dawsari took the ball out of the air on the edge of the box, danced past both Nahuel Molina and Ángel Di María, and curled a right-footed shot high into the far top corner past Emiliano Martínez — a goal of the tournament contender that completed the comeback. Sky's call: 'Time stood still as Al-Dawsari plucked the ball out from the sky and turned inside two Argentina defenders before curling his finish beyond the reach of Aston Villa goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez.' Saudi fans chanted 'Our team fulfils our dreams!'
magic_moment.why: The decisive winner and the image of the upset — a 0.05-xG strike (per soccer-blogger) of breathtaking individual quality that beat one of the world's best keepers and the eventual world champions.

magic_moment.text: Three minutes into the second half, Al-Shehri pounced on hesitancy from Cristian Romero, cut inside and flashed a low right-footed shot across Martínez into the bottom corner to level at 1-1 — Saudi Arabia's first shot on target of the match and the goal that flipped the script.
magic_moment.why: The equaliser that broke the dam: Saudi's first real chance, taken clinically, igniting the five-minute window that won the game.

stats.text: Argentina generated ~2.16 xG (xgscore.io) to ~2.29 (soccer-blogger) — a dominant chance profile, yet they lost. Models differ by provider; both put Argentina well above 2.0 xG.

Saudi Arabia won on just 0.14 xG per Opta — the lowest xG a team has needed to win a World Cup match since 1966 (after Japan's 0.20 vs Cameroon in 2010). xgscore.io's model has it at 0.35. Either way, the lowest-quality-chances side won.

stats.value: Argentina 15 (6 on target); Saudi Arabia 3 (2 on target)
stats.text: Argentina out-shot Saudi Arabia 15 to 3. Saudi Arabia put just two shots on target all match — and scored from both. Ruthless conversion against overwhelming territorial dominance.

Argentina held 69% possession with 596 passes at 85% accuracy vs Saudi Arabia's 266 passes at 68%. Control of the ball did not translate into control of the result — Saudi's deep-block-after-leading plus high-line offside trap absorbed it.

stats.value: 10 total (7 before half-time; 6 in first 32 min); 3 goals disallowed
stats.text: Argentina were flagged offside seven times before half-time — six of them inside the first 32 minutes, more than any team recorded in a full match at the 2018 World Cup — and had three goals chalked off by semi-automated offside technology. The defining hard number of the upset: the high line, not the keeper, beat Argentina.

pre_match.market_prob_basis: De-vigged from Caesars Sportsbook three-way moneyline (via CBS Sports): Argentina -210, Draw +285, Mexico +700. Raw implied: ARG 0.6774, Draw 0.2597, MEX 0.1250 (overround 1.0621). De-vigged Argentina win prob = 0.6774 / 1.0621 = 0.638 ≈ 0.64. Despite the shock opening loss to Saudi Arabia, the market still had Argentina as clear favourites over a defensive Mexico.

outcome.method: Two goals in open play (Messi 65', Enzo Fernández 87')

odds.system: Bookmaker de-vig (Caesars Sportsbook three-way moneyline, via CBS Sports)
odds.text: Pre-match Caesars three-way price had Argentina -210, Draw +285, Mexico +700. Removing the 6.2% overround yields a de-vigged Argentina win probability of ~0.64. Even after the Saudi Arabia upset, the market kept Argentina firm favourites: a must-win that the favourite was still expected to take ~2-in-3 of the time.

narrative.storyline: Mexico's defensive 5-3-2 stifled Argentina until it backfired
narrative.text: Tata Martino abandoned his usual 4-3-3 for a defensive 5-3-2, packing numbers in central areas. It initially frustrated La Albiceleste, but in the second half Argentina exploited the shape on the flanks — Jesús Gallardo 'looked overwhelmed when Argentina roamed onto his area' — and the structure that had kept the first half scoreless ultimately cracked.
narrative.why: The match was decided as much by Mexico's containment plan collapsing in the second half as by Argentine quality; the tactical tweak that worked for 64 minutes failed at the decisive moment.

narrative.storyline: A must-win after the Saudi shock — 'another World Cup starts'
narrative.text: The opening defeat to Saudi Arabia meant defeat here would have all but eliminated Argentina after two games, ending Messi's final World Cup bid. Messi framed the stakes himself: 'After the goal, we became again who we are... we needed this result, we needed this euphoria in this game that we had to win.'
narrative.why: Motivation and pressure were the central human story: this was effectively a knockout game disguised as a group fixture, and the psychological release after Messi's goal reset the entire tournament for Argentina.

narrative.storyline: An attritional, record-low-quality contest broken by one moment
narrative.text: The first half was the lowest-quality of the entire tournament to that point — barely any clear chances, with Opta logging just ~0.05 xG for Argentina and ~0.07 for Mexico across the opening 45 (the lowest combined first-half xG of the 2022 World Cup). Argentina dominated the ball (67.3% first-half possession) but their 'boring possession' recalled the laboured 2018 midfield until Messi's strike unlocked it.
narrative.why: Frames why the favourite needed individual brilliance rather than sustained chance creation: the game state was a low-event stalemate where one piece of magic, not territorial dominance, was always likely to be the difference.

narrative.storyline: Enzo Fernández announces himself; Messi turns provider
narrative.text: Substitute Enzo Fernández (on from the 57th minute) sealed it in the 87th, cutting inside from the left after a Messi-worked corner and curling 'a sumptuous finish' past Guillermo Ochoa — at 21, becoming Argentina's youngest World Cup scorer since Messi in 2006, with Messi himself supplying the assist.
narrative.why: The killer second goal marked the emergence of a future Argentina midfield star and showed Messi shifting from scorer to creator — a generational handover moment inside the result.

magic_moment.text: With the game deadlocked, Di María rolled it to Messi ~25 yards out and Messi rifled a low, precise strike into the bottom corner past Ochoa — his 93rd Argentina goal and 8th at World Cups, equalling Diego Maradona's tally. The Lusail crowd erupted; it was the single moment that revived Argentina's whole campaign.
magic_moment.why: This is the node's decisive moment: a near-elimination must-win, broken by a vintage Messi long-ranger that swung Argentina's tournament from the brink back to favourites.

magic_moment.text: Three minutes from time, substitute Enzo Fernández cut inside from the left off a Messi-assisted corner and curled a sumptuous finish into the far top corner past Ochoa — a goal pundits said 'rivalled Messi's' — to make it 2-0 and secure the result beyond doubt.
magic_moment.why: The insurance goal that confirmed the win and depended only on Argentina themselves; a star-is-born moment for the 21-year-old.

stats.text: Per-side full-match xG: Argentina 0.53, Mexico 0.37. Both sides drastically over-performed their chance quality — Argentina scored twice from just 0.53 xG, underlining that the result hinged on finishing quality (Messi's long-ranger) rather than chance volume.

stats.value: Argentina 5 shots (2 on target) — Mexico 4 shots (1 on target)
stats.text: Argentina took just 5 shots, only 2 on target — and scored from both — while Mexico managed 4 shots, 1 on target. A remarkably low-event game; Argentina's finishing efficiency, not shot dominance, decided it.
Argentina controlled possession 58%–42% across the match (and 67.3% in the first half per Opta), but that territorial dominance produced very little clear-cut threat until Messi's strike.

stats.value: 0.28 combined (ARG ~0.05, MEX ~0.07 in some splits) — lowest first half of the tournament
stats.text: The opening 45 produced the lowest combined first-half xG of the entire 2022 World Cup, and the full match's combined xG (0.54 by Opta's model) was the lowest of any game in the tournament — an attritional stalemate broken by individual quality.

stats.value: 93rd Argentina goal; 8th World Cup goal (equalled Maradona)
stats.text: Messi's 65th-minute strike was his 93rd goal in 168 appearances for Argentina and his 8th at a World Cup, equalling Diego Maradona's career World Cup goal tally — historical weight that amplified the moment's significance.

pre_match.market_prob_basis: De-vigged from the pre-match three-way bookmaker moneyline (Caesars, via CBS Sports): Argentina -225, Draw +305, Poland +700. Raw implied = 0.692 / 0.247 / 0.125 (overround 1.064); normalised Argentina win = 0.692 / 1.064 = 0.65. This converges almost exactly with Opta's supercomputer pre-match number (64.8%), giving two independent systems at ~0.65.

outcome.method: Regulation (group-stage win); second-half goals Mac Allister 46', Álvarez 67'

odds.system: Opta supercomputer (10,000-sim match model) cross-checked against bookmaker de-vig
odds.text: Two independent prediction systems agreed Argentina were clear but not overwhelming favourites in a win-or-bust group decider. The Opta supercomputer gave Argentina a 64.8% win probability, Poland 13.8%, and a draw 21.4%. De-vigging the Caesars pre-match moneyline (Argentina -225, Draw +305, Poland +700) yields a normalised Argentina win probability of ~0.65 — essentially identical to Opta. The market never priced this as a one-sided lock because Poland only needed a draw to advance and an Argentina defeat meant elimination, raising the stakes asymmetrically.

narrative.storyline: Scaloni's positional fluidity overwhelmed a passive Poland block
narrative.text: Argentina lined up in a fluid 4-3-1-2 with Messi roaming centrally and Álvarez replacing Lautaro Martínez for extra mobility, while Poland sat in a deep, compact 4-4-1-1 designed purely to limit Argentina's chances. Scaloni's licence for his players to drift off their nominal positions pulled Poland's lines apart; Argentina recorded their highest-ever World Cup passing volume (800 passes, 92% completion, since 1966), suffocating Poland into 27% possession and zero shots on target.
narrative.why: This is the tactical 'why' behind the scoreline — not luck but a deliberate fluid-possession structure dismantling a low block.

narrative.storyline: Messi's best tournament display so far — the penalty miss didn't break him
narrative.text: Messi produced his standout performance of Qatar 2022 — 98 touches, five dribbles, five chances created, involved in almost every attack — even though Szczęsny brilliantly saved his VAR-awarded first-half penalty. The human storyline was Argentina's composure: rather than letting the miss derail them, they came out and scored within a minute of the restart. Mac Allister said the side resolved to 'stay positive, to stay calm' after the spot-kick.
narrative.why: Distinct from tactics — the key-player and psychology arc that defined the match's mood and Messi's redemption framing.

narrative.storyline: Poland survived by goal difference while being thoroughly outplayed — the cynical-survival subplot
narrative.text: Poland advanced in second place purely on goal difference over Mexico, and coach Czesław Michniewicz openly instructed his players to 'avoid silly bookings' to protect a fair-play / goal-difference tiebreak as news of Saudi Arabia v Mexico filtered through. Lewandowski did not register a single shot. The narrative wasn't Poland's resistance but their pragmatic, almost passive, qualification by the back door.
narrative.why: The losing side's motivation story — qualifying by tiebreak math, not performance — a separate human/strategic thread from Argentina's dominance.

magic_moment.text: 46' — Alexis Mac Allister opened the scoring within a minute of the restart, meeting Nahuel Molina's low cut-back from the right with a first-time, slightly scuffed finish that trickled past Szczęsny and in off the far post. The timing was the broadcast story: it instantly washed away the first-half frustration of the missed Messi penalty and released the dam Argentina had been building.
magic_moment.why: The decisive opener — it converted total territorial dominance into a lead at the psychologically perfect moment, right after the penalty miss.

magic_moment.text: 67' — Julián Álvarez collected an Enzo Fernández pass and curled a brilliant left-footed finish past Szczęsny to make it 2-0, killing the contest and confirming Argentina would top Group C.
magic_moment.why: The killer second goal — sealed the group win and underlined Álvarez's emergence as the mobile striker Scaloni's system needed.

stats.text: Argentina generated nearly 10x Poland's xG, the clearest measure of how lopsided the chance creation was.

stats.value: Argentina 23 shots (12 on target) — Poland 4 shots (0 on target)
stats.text: Poland did not register a single shot on target across 90 minutes; Lewandowski had no shots at all.
Argentina monopolised the ball, pinning Poland into a deep block for almost the entire match.
Poland's 0.00 xGOT confirms they never tested the goalkeeper; Argentina's 3.02 reflects high-quality, on-frame shooting.

stats.value: Argentina 800 passes at 92% completion (their highest in any World Cup match since 1966)
stats.text: A record-setting passing performance that quantifies Scaloni's possession-dominance plan.

nodes.competition: 2022 FIFA World Cup, Final — Lusail Iconic Stadium, Qatar

pre_match.market_prob_basis: De-vigged from the two-way 'to lift the trophy' market (includes extra time + penalties), the cleanest single-side win price for this match. CBS Sports listed Argentina -125 / France +100. Raw implied: Argentina -125 = 0.5556, France +100 = 0.5000; overround 1.0556; de-vigged Argentina = 0.5556 / 1.0556 = 0.526. Note: the 90-minute 3-way moneyline (FOX Bet: France +175, Argentina +162, Draw +190) made France the nominal regulation favourite, but on the only market that settles who actually wins the match (incl. ET/pens), Argentina was the slight favourite — consistent with the seed's 'even / slight Argentina'. The match was a near coin-flip.

outcome.score: Argentina 3–3 France after extra time; Argentina won 4–2 on penalties
outcome.method: penalty shootout (after 2–2 in 90', 3–3 after extra time)

odds.system: bookmaker de-vig (two-way trophy market) — CBS Sports / SportsLine odds feed
odds.text: On the market that actually settles the match (win the trophy, including extra time and penalties), Argentina was the slight favourite at -125 with France at +100 (CBS Sports). De-vigging the two prices (Argentina 0.5556, France 0.5000; overround 1.0556) yields a calibrated ~52.6% win probability for Argentina — effectively a coin-flip. This contrasts with the 90-minute 3-way moneyline (FOX Bet: France +175, Argentina +162, Draw +190), where the high draw probability made France the nominal regulation favourite. The market read the two sides as near-equals; Argentina was favoured only once extra time/penalties were priced in.

narrative.storyline: Scaloni's tactical ambush — Di María recalled to torture Koundé
narrative.text: Lionel Scaloni's decisive call was reinstating Ángel Di María on the left, where he repeatedly isolated and beat right-back Jules Koundé. Di María won the first-half penalty (drawing the foul on Ousmane Dembélé's side) and finished the sweeping team move for 2–0. Argentina pressed France's build-up aggressively and forced a passive, shot-less first half from the holders — France did not register a single shot until the 70th minute.
narrative.why: The tactical plan, not a moment of magic, is what put Argentina 2–0 up and in control for 80 minutes — it defined the shape of the entire match.

narrative.storyline: France's no-show first half and Deschamps' emergency double substitution
narrative.text: France were anonymous for an hour: Olivier Giroud and Dembélé were so ineffective that Didier Deschamps hooked both before half-time — a near-unprecedented move in a World Cup final — sending on Marcus Thuram and Randal Kolo Muani. France became the first team since at least 1966 not to attempt a shot in the first half of a World Cup final. The substitutions ultimately revived them: Kolo Muani won the 80th-minute penalty and Thuram set up Mbappé's second.
narrative.why: France's collapse and Deschamps' desperate early gamble explain how a 2–0 deficit became the launchpad for the greatest final comeback — a distinct human/management storyline from the tactics.

narrative.storyline: Messi's coronation vs Mbappé's defiance — the generational duel
narrative.text: The final was framed as Messi's last shot at the trophy that defined Maradona's legacy against Mbappé's claim to the throne. Messi scored in regulation (penalty) and in extra time (108'), captaining Argentina to the title in his fifth and final World Cup and winning the Golden Ball. Mbappé answered with a hat-trick — the first in a World Cup final since 1966 — and took the Golden Boot with 8 goals. Both stars scored in the shootout; only Messi left with the trophy.
narrative.why: The personal stakes — Messi's career-defining title vs Mbappé's heir-apparent statement — are the human core that made this 'the greatest final ever', separate from any tactical or statistical read.

narrative.storyline: Emiliano Martínez, the shootout specialist who tilted the margins
narrative.text: Argentina's edge in the decisive phases ran through goalkeeper Emiliano 'Dibu' Martínez: his sprawling 123rd-minute save to deny Kolo Muani's near-certain winner (≈0.27 xG chance) kept Argentina alive, and in the shootout he saved Kingsley Coman's penalty and gamesmanship'd Aurélien Tchouaméni into missing. France converted only 2 of 4. Argentina's calm from the spot (4/4 from Messi, Dybala, Paredes, Montiel) closed it out.
narrative.why: The match was decided in the phases models can't fully capture — a last-gasp save and a shootout edge — and Martínez was the difference-maker in both, a separate turning-point storyline.

magic_moment.text: Mbappé's 97-second brace, 80'–81'. Trailing 2–0 and shotless, France struck twice in under two minutes: Mbappé buried an 80th-minute penalty (won by Kolo Muani off Otamendi) past Emi Martínez, then 97 seconds later collected a give-and-go with Thuram and thundered a first-time volley into the bottom corner for 2–2. It is the fastest two-goal swing in any World Cup final and ripped the trophy out of Argentina's hands.
magic_moment.why: This is the broadcast moment that turned a procession into the greatest final ever — the comeback that forced extra time and ultimately penalties.

magic_moment.text: Messi's 108th-minute extra-time goal. Lautaro Martínez's shot was parried by Lloris and Messi pounced to bundle it over the line (initially flagged, then awarded) for 3–2 — what looked like the title-winning goal and Messi's coronation, before Mbappé's 118th-minute penalty (his hat-trick) dragged it to a shootout.
magic_moment.why: Messi's putative championship goal, the emotional peak of his career — even though Mbappé's hat-trick penalty meant it didn't settle it.

magic_moment.text: Emi Martínez's 123rd-minute save from Kolo Muani. Deep into extra time at 3–3, Mbappé sent Kolo Muani clean through; the striker shot low and hard but Martínez stuck out his left leg to deflect it wide — a ≈0.27 xG chance saved, the last action that decided the match would go to penalties rather than to France.
magic_moment.why: The single defensive moment that kept Argentina in the World Cup; without it France win in open play. Iconic in StatsBomb's match retrospectives.

stats.text: Across the full 120 minutes Argentina out-created France 3.45 to 2.29 xG. France's total was inflated by two penalties; their non-penalty xG at full-time (90') was just 0.29.

Argentina utterly dominated the opening 45 minutes by xG, 1.49 to 0.00 — France did not register a single shot in the first half, the first team since at least 1966 to fail to do so in a World Cup final.

stats.value: Argentina 21 (10 on target) — France 10 (5 on target)
stats.text: Argentina more than doubled France's shot volume and on-target count, reflecting their territorial and chance-creation dominance across the match.
Argentina controlled the ball, 54% to 46%, with 635 passes at 83% accuracy versus France's 532 passes at 77% — they dictated tempo for long stretches.

stats.metric: Big chance saved / GK decisive intervention
stats.value: Martínez 120'+ save ≈ 0.27 xG denied; shootout 1 save (Coman) + Tchouaméni miss forced
stats.text: Emiliano Martínez's late save denied Kolo Muani a ≈0.27 xG near-certain winner, and in the shootout he saved Coman and pressured Tchouaméni into missing — France converted only 2 of 4 spot-kicks to Argentina's 4 of 4.

Belgium de-vig = 0.512/1.056 = 0.485. Belgium was the nominal favourite (FIFA #2) but the line had drifted hard from -160 toward -105 pre-kickoff — Action Network reported Belgium 'were as high as -160 on the three-way moneyline, but are now as low as -105' (https://www.actionnetwork.com/soccer/belgium-vs-morocco-world-cup-odds-pick-take-this-angle-on-the-spread) — leaving the win priced as a near coin-flip.

odds.text: Belgium were the favourite but only marginally: FanDuel's pre-match three-way moneyline had Belgium -105, Draw +240, Morocco +300. After removing the 5.6% overround, Belgium's true win probability was ~48.5% — a near coin-flip, not a heavy favourite. Action Network reported the line had already drifted from as high as -160 toward -105, the market quietly fading Belgium before kickoff. The closing price effectively foreshadowed the upset.

narrative.storyline: Morocco's compact mid-block strangled Belgium's golden generation
narrative.text: Regragui set Morocco in a disciplined 4-1-4-1 mid-block, ceding the majority of possession but conceding nothing of value. Amrabat shadowed Hazard while Mazraoui tracked De Bruyne, forcing Belgium wide and isolating their playmakers in the half-spaces. Belgium's 'passive possession' produced volume without penetration. (Possession share — Belgium 67% — is carried in the stats layer; Breaking The Lines' own figure of 56% differs, so the exact split is sourced to xGscore/ESPN rather than this tactical piece.)
narrative.why: Explains how a side ranked #2 in the world was held to almost no clear chances despite two-thirds of the ball.

narrative.storyline: Belgium's stars were laboured and stifled — a golden generation fading
narrative.text: De Bruyne, Eden Hazard and Thorgan Hazard were all smothered; Belgium were 'comparatively laboured throughout, offering very little threat from their star marksmen.' The performance crystallised the sense that Martinez's aging generation had run its course at this World Cup.
narrative.why: The human/decline story: a top-2 side's elite attackers neutralised, framing the result as more than a one-off.

narrative.storyline: Ziyech's disallowed first-half goal was the suppressed turning point
narrative.text: Ziyech curled in a first-half free-kick that was chalked off for offside — Saiss was a fraction ahead and judged to be interfering with Courtois' eyeline. Morocco had effectively already breached Courtois from a set-piece once; the second time, in the 73rd minute, it stood.
narrative.why: Shows the winning goal wasn't luck: Morocco were repeatedly engineering set-piece danger against Courtois' near post.

narrative.storyline: Sabiri the unlikely architect — and Ziyech's Player-of-the-Match strings
narrative.text: Squad player Abdelhamid Sabiri delivered the decisive free-kick, while Hakim Ziyech was named Player of the Match, pulling the strings and assisting Aboukhlal's clincher. Morocco's depth, not just its defence, decided it.
narrative.why: Reframes the upset around individual contributions FIFA/Chelsea singled out, beyond the tactical structure.

magic_moment.text: 73' — Abdelhamid Sabiri's free-kick from the left was whipped in low and direct, a cross-cum-shot that dipped past Thibaut Courtois at his near post with Saiss pressuring on the line. A near-post 'nightmare' for one of the world's best keepers; Morocco had deliberately overloaded the near post after their earlier disallowed set-piece. (Note: ESPN's box score credits Saiss at the near post; FIFA and Goal credit Sabiri's direct free-kick — this node anchors on Sabiri per confirmed scorers.)
magic_moment.why: The breakthrough that beat an elite keeper and launched Morocco's historic run; the signature image of the upset.

magic_moment.text: 90+2' — Zakaria Aboukhlal sealed it in stoppage time, finishing an attacking transition from Hakim Ziyech's delivery to make it 2-0 and confirm Morocco's place atop Group F.
magic_moment.why: Killed off any Belgian comeback and turned a tight upset into a statement scoreline.

narrative.storyline: Deschamps' reactive 4-3-3 ceded the ball and won the game
narrative.text: France set up in a 4-3-3 with Tchouaméni as a single pivot and were content to sit deep — they had only ~39% possession yet attacked Morocco's 5-4-1 block through line-breaking passes from Varane/Koundé into Griezmann between the lines, leaning heavily on Mbappé's pace down the left. For the second game running Deschamps' side had less of the ball than their opponent and still controlled the result, a hallmark of his counter-punching France.
narrative.why: Explains how the favourite won on 39% possession — the result was a tactical design, not a fluke, and reinforced the de-vig favourite read.

narrative.storyline: Morocco's defensive injury crisis hollowed out their tournament-best back line
narrative.text: Morocco — who had conceded only one goal all tournament (an own goal) — were gutted at the back: Nayef Aguerd withdrew before kickoff despite being named to start, and captain Romain Saïss limped off after roughly 21 minutes, forcing Walid Regragui to abandon the planned back five. The reshuffle created the uncertainty France punished inside five minutes.
narrative.why: A distinct human/availability storyline (not tactics or odds) that materially shifted the contest the bookmakers had priced as tight.

narrative.storyline: Morocco actually pushed France hard — the xG gap was modest and they hit the post
narrative.system: Breaking The Lines / Sky Sports (chances analysis)
narrative.text: The Atlas Lions were far from passive: Jawad El Yamiq struck the post with an acrobatic overhead kick, substitute Abderrazak Hamdallah hesitated on multiple openings inside the box, and Azzedine Ounahi fired over in stoppage time. Morocco generated 1.21 xG to France's 2.17 — a single concession away from a different game, validating the seed note that they 'pushed France hard.'
narrative.why: Counter-balances the 2–0 scoreline, showing the match was more contested than the result and aligning with the modest xG margin in the stats layer.

narrative.storyline: A place in history — France into back-to-back finals
narrative.text: Victory made France the first nation to reach consecutive World Cup finals since Brazil in 2002, setting up the Argentina final and a chance to become the first European side to win back-to-back titles since Germany in 1990. It also ended Morocco's run as the first African and first Arab nation to reach a World Cup semi-final.
narrative.why: The stakes/legacy storyline that defined the fixture's meaning beyond the scoreline.

magic_moment.text: Theo Hernández opened the scoring after only 4 minutes 39 seconds — the fastest goal in a World Cup semi-final since Vavá for Brazil vs France in 1958. Jawad El Yamiq's failed interception of Varane's pass to Griezmann let the ball break loose; Mbappé's effort was blocked and Hernández acrobatically swept the rebound high past Bono from a tight angle — the first goal Morocco had conceded from open play all tournament.
magic_moment.why: The decisive early blow — it forced ball-shy Morocco to chase the game against a France side built to counter, and instantly set the match script.

magic_moment.text: Randal Kolo Muani sealed it on 79' just 44 seconds after coming off the bench — the third-fastest substitute goal in World Cup history. Mbappé jinked into the box and his deflected shot rolled across the face of goal for Kolo Muani to tap in at the far post for his first international goal, killing the contest.
magic_moment.why: The clincher — an instant-impact substitute goal that ended Morocco's hopes of a late comeback and confirmed France's final berth.

odds.text: Germany entered as a clear favourite. FanDuel priced GER -210 / Draw +350 / JPN +550; de-vigging the three-way book (overround 1.0534) gives Germany a 0.643 win probability, Draw 0.211, Japan 0.146. Other books agreed Germany was ~64-71% (Fox Sports -227, Caesars -245). The market gave Japan only a ~15% raw chance — making the 1–2 result a genuine upset against the closing-style price.

narrative.storyline: Moriyasu's halftime/second-half shape change 4-2-3-1 → 3-4-3 unlocked the game
narrative.text: Japan's manager Hajime Moriyasu switched from 4-2-3-1 to a 3-4-3, introducing Takehiro Tomiyasu as a left-sided centre-back and activating wing-backs as attacking weapons. The change let Japan push more bodies forward, create numerical overloads in the half-spaces (left wing-back + left centre-back), and finally control possession in spells — the platform that broke Germany's block in the final 15 minutes.
narrative.why: It identifies the single decision that turned a 73%-possession defeat into a win: a structural switch, not luck.

narrative.storyline: Germany's historic profligacy — dominated every metric and still lost
narrative.text: Opta framed this as a statistical anomaly: it was the first World Cup match since at least 1966 in which a team surpassed three expected goals and lost. Germany registered ~76% possession, exceeded 3.0 xG, and Manuel Neuer set a tournament record with 51 completed passes — none of which prevented the upset. The result echoed South Korea's 2-0 win over Germany in 2018, both with the winners holding similarly low possession.
narrative.why: Quantifies WHY the favourite lost: elite chance creation undone by zero clinical edge — the core 'dominate-and-lose' story.

narrative.storyline: Bench-driven turnaround and Flick's own verdict on efficiency
narrative.text: Both Japan goals came from substitutes — Bundesliga-based Ritsu Doan and Takuma Asano — introduced to transform the final 15 minutes despite Japan's ~24% possession. Hansi Flick conceded the loss plainly: 'We deserved to go in front... then Japan gave us a lesson in efficiency.' Goalkeeper Shuichi Gonda's saves kept Japan in it long enough for the bench to strike.
narrative.why: The human/management angle: a losing manager's admission plus the squad-depth contrast that decided it.

narrative.storyline: The German-based core comes home to haunt Germany
narrative.text: Japan's match-winners were schooled in the Bundesliga: Doan (Freiburg) and Asano (then Bochum) struck against the country whose league shaped them — Asano's near-post finish carrying symbolic weight after his Freiburg side had lost 7-0 to Neuer's Bayern months earlier. Eight German-based players featured in Japan's squad, and that familiarity with German football fed the late breakthrough.
narrative.why: A distinct human narrative thread (familiarity/symbolism) separate from the tactics and stats stories.

magic_moment.text: Manuel Neuer parried Takumi Minamino's strike straight into the path of substitute Ritsu Doan, who hammered the rebound home to make it 1–1 with 15 minutes left — the goal that flipped the emotional momentum of the match.
magic_moment.why: The release moment: it turned a controlled German lead into a live contest and set up the winner.

magic_moment.text: Substitute Takuma Asano latched onto a long ball over the top, sprinted clear of Nico Schlotterbeck, took a touch and rifled a finish past Neuer from a tight near-post angle — Japan's first-ever win over Germany and the signature image of the upset. (İlkay Gündoğan had opened the scoring from a 33' penalty after David Raum was fouled.)
magic_moment.why: The decisive goal — a brilliant individual finish from a narrow angle that beat Neuer and won the match.
